sections.content:
The reason the dictionary comprehension failed is that I was using a tuple (r,c) as the value, and then trying to index into ym['Y']... The actual error: KeyError 'Y' — because the dict comprehension `{c:(r,c) for c,r,c in squares}` — the loop variables are c, r, c — the second c shadows the first! So the key becomes the column integer, not the color. That's the bug. The squares are: M is at (58,38), Y is at (58,52). Wait, but the earlier ASCII showed M at columns 49-52 and Y at 61-64? The segmentation says M center (58,38), Y (58,52). Hmm, the ASCII row 57: "cccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccMMMMccccccccccYYYYccccccccc" — 29 c's, then MMMM at columns 29-32? But the segmentation says M is at 38. Oh well — I'll trust the segmentation (the ASCII might be from a slightly different row). Actually, the ASCII row shown: counting the c's: "ccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccc" = 29, then MMMM (29-32), then "cccccccccc" 12 c's (33-44), YYYY (45-48), then 9 c's. That would put M at 29-32, Y at 45-48. But the segmentation says M center column 38, Y center column 52. Contradiction — maybe the ASCII row I'm reading is row 57 and the squares are at rows 57-60... The boundary corners might be (57,36)-(60,40) → center (58,38). The ASCII display might be off. I'll trust the segmentation.
Anyway, the state hasn't changed (no action was executed due to the exception). Next, I'll execute: click Y (58,52) → green3 (36,34); click M (58,38) → green4 (36,40); SPACE.
